name: Chlormadinone acetate

lead: Chlormadinone acetate is a prescription progestin with antiandrogenic effects, found mainly in combined contraceptive pills such as Belara sold outside the US. Doctors use these pills for women with acne, oily skin or excess hair who also want contraception.

It blocks the androgen receptor and suppresses LH and FSH, lowering androgen effects in skin and hair follicles, so there is less sebum and clearer skin. Acne evidence comes from open-label studies, including one of an ethinylestradiol/CMA pill over 12 cycles; no large randomized acne trial was found.

paras: It is taken as a combined daily pill chosen by a prescriber, and benefits on skin are generally judged over several months of cycles.

Low-dose pills commonly cause irregular bleeding, headache, nausea and breast tenderness. High doses have been linked to adrenal and metabolic effects, and prolonged high-dose use to meningioma. It is prescription-only and was withdrawn in the US around 1970 after dog mammary tumour findings.

angle.text: Chlormadinone acetate blocks the androgen receptor, so skin makes less sebum and breakouts and oiliness ease. Women use pills containing it for acne and oily skin. Support comes from open-label studies.

lead: Chlormadinone acetate (CMA) is a synthetic progestin derived from 17-hydroxyprogesterone. It has progestogenic activity together with antiandrogenic effects, acting both by blocking the androgen receptor and by lowering gonadotropin-driven hormone production.[1][2][3] It is mostly used at 2 mg in combined oral contraceptives with ethinylestradiol (for example Belara), in some menopausal hormone therapies, and at higher doses for prostate conditions in Japan and South Korea.[1][2]

In the appearance context, CMA-containing pills are prescribed to women who want contraception and also have acne, oily skin, seborrhea, hirsutism or female pattern hair loss, in the same way cyproterone acetate or drospirenone pills are.[1][2] By reducing androgen signalling at the oil glands and hair follicles, the pill is intended to leave skin clearer and less oily and to ease androgen-driven hair changes.[3] Women using it report and trials measure changes in acne lesion counts, sebum, pore size, hair quality and hirsutism scores.[4][5][6][7]

Human research includes a single-blind randomized phase III trial in 199 women compared with a levonorgestrel pill, a double-blind placebo-controlled phase III trial in moderate acne, a 180-woman randomized comparison with a drospirenone pill, open-label studies of skin and hair quality, and a polycystic ovary syndrome trial.[4][5][8][9][6][7] A French national cohort has also linked prolonged CMA use to a higher risk of intracranial meningioma, which has led to regulatory attention in Europe.[10]
It is not marketed in the United States, where combination products were discontinued in the early 1970s after mammary findings in dogs.[1]
infobox: Acne, seborrhea, hirsutism and pattern hair loss in women, as part of contraceptive pills[1][3]
2 mg CMA with 0.02 or 0.03 mg ethinylestradiol[2]
Belara, Belarina, Gynorelle, Luteran, Lutoral, Prostal[1]
Prescription-only; not marketed in the US, UK, Canada, Australia or Nordic countries[1]

paras: Wikipedia lists acne, hirsutism, seborrhea and pattern hair loss among androgen-dependent conditions for which CMA has been used in women.[1] Reviews of antiandrogenic progestogens describe chlormadinone acetate, cyproterone acetate and dienogest as pills that provide contraception while offering benefits for androgen-related skin conditions, including a reduction in activity of skin 5-alpha-reductase.[3] A 2003 review of systemic acne treatment discusses antiandrogenic hormonal options in this area.[11]

In practice, the CMA pill is chosen for women who need contraception and also want help with oily skin, breakouts, excess facial or body hair or scalp seborrhea. Studies of the 2 mg CMA with 0.03 mg ethinylestradiol pill have followed acne lesion counts, sebum levels, pore size, hair density and quality-of-life questionnaires.[5][6][7] Grokipedia describes EE/CMA studies reporting reductions in acne severity and oiliness over 12 treatment cycles in women aged 16 to 45, and use in hyperandrogenic conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome.[2] In the long-term Belara contraceptive study of 1,655 women, investigators also recorded the influence of the pill on acne and seborrhea as clinical signs of androgenisation.[12]
Topical CMA has been tried too. A 1970 report in Acta Dermato-Venereologica studied the antiandrogen chlormadinone acetate applied topically in acne and reported a lack of effect.[13]

CMA at 2 mg with 0.02 or 0.03 mg ethinylestradiol is a contraceptive, with reported adjusted Pearl indices from about 0.04 to 0.33.[2] It is also used in menopausal hormone therapy, in gynaecological disorders such as irregular or painful bleeding and endometriosis (for example in France as Luteran), and for prostate cancer and benign prostatic hyperplasia mainly in Japan and South Korea.[1][2] Wikipedia also lists precocious puberty in girls and use in hormone therapy for transgender women, mostly in Japan.[1]

The 2001 Dermatology trial was single-blind, randomized and multicentre, and enrolled 199 female acne patients to compare EE/CMA with EE/levonorgestrel in mild to moderate papulopustular acne of the face and acne-related disorders.[4] The 2009 Contraception trial was randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled, testing the 0.03 mg EE and 2 mg CMA pill (Belara) in moderate acne.[5] A 2004 Drugs review covers the combination as a whole.[14]

The contraceptive efficacy data are extensive: a phase III open study followed 1,655 women over 22,337 cycles, and shorter studies tracked cycle control and safety over three cycles.[12][15] Experts note that real-world effectiveness depends on adherence.[2]

CMA is a progesterone receptor agonist, an androgen receptor antagonist (with weak partial agonism) and an antigonadotropin that suppresses LH and FSH; it has weak glucocorticoid activity and no estrogenic or antimineralocorticoid activity.[1] Relative to progesterone it has about 330 times the potency in the Clauberg test, and its antiandrogenic potency in animals is about a fifth of cyproterone acetate's.[1] Wikipedia reports that in men with benign prostatic hyperplasia a high oral dose lowered testosterone by roughly three quarters or more, illustrating its antigonadotropic action.[1]

By blocking androgen receptors, reducing skin 5-alpha-reductase activity and lowering ovarian and adrenal androgen production, it reduces androgen signalling at sebaceous glands and hair follicles.[3] Wikipedia notes that, unlike some 19-nortestosterone progestins, it does not raise sex hormone-binding globulin with ethinylestradiol, and that it does not inhibit cytochrome P450 enzymes.[1] A 1988 laboratory study compared the androgenic activity of several synthetic progestins in mouse cells, and reviews classify CMA among progestogens with antiandrogenic properties.[16][17][3][18]

Per Wikipedia, oral bioavailability is close to 100 percent, steady state is reached in 7 to 15 days, and the elimination half-life is roughly 25 to 89 hours. It is highly protein bound, metabolised in the liver to active hydroxylated metabolites, and excreted in urine and faeces.[1]

Acne, controlled trials. A single-blind, randomized, controlled, parallel phase III trial compared EE/CMA (Belara) with EE/levonorgestrel (Microgynon) in 199 female acne patients with mild to moderate papulopustular facial acne.[4] A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial tested the 0.03 mg EE/2 mg CMA pill in moderate acne.[5] A 2018 investigator-blinded randomized trial at Chulalongkorn University in Bangkok enrolled 180 women with acne and dysmenorrhea and compared EE/CMA with EE/drospirenone; at month 6 total acne lesions had fallen by 72.2 percent with CMA and 64.5 percent with drospirenone, investigator-rated improvement was excellent in 75.3 and 49.4 percent respectively, and adverse events did not differ significantly.[8]

Skin and androgen signs, comparisons. A randomized study of 55 women with oily skin, acne or excess hair compared EE/drospirenone (30 women) with EE/CMA (25 women) over six months. Both pills lowered circulating androgens and raised SHBG and improved skin condition, and the drospirenone combination produced greater improvement in oily skin, acne, hair growth and hormonal measures in that study.[19] Different trials in different populations have therefore compared CMA with drospirenone and reached different conclusions.[8][19]

Skin and hair, open-label. A 2008 single-centre phase IV study followed 44 women aged 18 to 37 for six cycles of the EE/CMA pill and reported significantly improved clinical acne scores with fewer comedones, papules and seborrhea, smaller pores, better barrier function and higher stratum corneum hydration.[6] A 2013 phase IV study enrolled 60 women, analysed 31, and reported improved scalp and forehead sebum excretion, an increased number of terminal hairs, fewer signs of scalp seborrhea and dandruff, and better self-rated hair quality over 12 cycles.[7]

Hirsutism and polycystic ovary syndrome. A clinical trial of EE/CMA in normal-weight women with PCOS reported that hirsutism improved, SHBG rose, free androgen index and androstenedione fell, and glucose, insulin and most lipid measures were unchanged after six cycles.[9] A registered safety study of hormonal contraceptives in 75 women with PCOS also exists.[20]

Contraception. An open, noncontrolled phase III study followed 1,655 women taking the pill for 22,337 cycles, also observing acne and seborrhea;[12] a phase II study evaluated efficacy and safety over three cycles.[15]

Other registered trials include a comparison of body weight change during contraception with Belara versus Yasmin (100 participants), a postmenopausal hormone therapy study of progestagen type and gene expression (40 participants), and a large retrospective venous thromboembolism cohort.[21][22][23] A review of hormonal contraceptives for dysmenorrhea also covers this drug class.[24] A 1971 report examined a sequential mestranol-chlormadinone combination in female acne.[25]

With low-dose combined pills, Wikipedia lists menstrual irregularities, headache, nausea, breast tenderness and vaginal discharge.[1] At high doses, reduced libido, reduced body hair, adrenal insufficiency on abrupt discontinuation and altered carbohydrate metabolism have been reported, and with estrogen in menopausal therapy breast cancer risk is increased.[1] CMA is a teratogen in animals and may feminise male fetuses.[1]

Wikipedia states that CMA does not appear to raise venous thromboembolism risk on its own; a registered retrospective cohort study (RIVET) has examined venous thromboembolism risk with hormonal contraceptives in about 124,000 participants.[1][21] Reviews of progestogen risks discuss effects on lipids, clotting factors and blood pressure for the drug class.[26]

A French population-based cohort study published in the European Journal of Neurology in 2025 followed 828,499 women aged 10 to 70 who started CMA between 2007 and 2017. Meningioma surgery or radiotherapy occurred at 18.5 per 100,000 person-years in 469,976 women with a cumulative dose above 360 mg in the first six months, versus 6.8 in 358,523 comparison women, an age-adjusted relative risk of 3.1; in the highest cumulative-dose group the adjusted relative risk was 6.9. The authors reported a strong dose-effect relationship and that CMA-associated meningiomas were more often at the skull base.[10]

Case reports describe meningioma in CMA users, including a grade 3 anaplastic meningioma.[27] Commentators have also urged measured communication about the risk for women using pills with nomegestrol or chlormadinone, arguing against alarm.[28] Grokipedia states that prolonged high-dose CMA exposure has been associated with elevated meningioma risk, similar to other progestins.[2]

Mammary nodules and tumours were seen in beagle dogs at 10 to 25 times the human dose over two to four years, and CMA-containing products were withdrawn in the US in 1971 and 1972; later research did not find a similar risk in humans, according to Wikipedia.[1]

CMA is a pregnane steroid derived from 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone, with a chlorine at carbon 6, a double bond between carbons 6 and 7 and a 17-alpha acetate ester. It differs from cyproterone acetate only in lacking the 1-alpha,2-alpha methylene group.[1] Its developmental code is RS-1280.[1]

Related 17-hydroxyprogesterone derivatives appeared in the mid-1950s, and CMA was first described in 1959 and introduced for medical use in 1965. Eli Lilly sold it with mestranol as C-Quens in the US from 1965 to 1971, the first sequential contraceptive pill in the US.[1] Its antiandrogenic activity was first described in 1966, according to Wikipedia.[1] Grokipedia dates its first synthesis to 1961.[2]

Mammary nodules and tumours in beagle dogs at 10 to 25 times the human dose led to C-Quens being voluntarily withdrawn in 1971, and US products with CMA were discontinued by 1972; CMA remained widely used in other countries such as Germany.[1] Early dermatology reports from 1970 and 1971 examined chlormadinone in acne topically and in a sequential pill.[13][25]

Interest in CMA for skin returned in the 1990s with the Belara pill (0.03 mg ethinylestradiol with 2 mg CMA), whose phase III trials, published from 1998, assessed acne and seborrhea alongside contraception.[12][4] Skin and hair studies of the pill followed in 2008 and 2013, and a randomized comparison with drospirenone in 2018.[6][7][8]

Brand names include Belara (Germany, Brazil), Belarina, Gynorelle, Luteran (France), Lutoral (Mexico), Prostal (Japan) and Prostal-L (South Korea), among many others, and veterinary brands also exist.[1] It is sold alone in France, Germany, Japan, Mexico and South Korea and in combination pills across much of Europe, Latin America and parts of Asia and the Middle East.[1] It is prescription-only and is not marketed in the US, UK, Canada, Australia or the Nordic countries.[1] Environmental studies have detected progestogens including CMA in aquatic environments and treated wastewater.[29][30]

Little community discussion of CMA was located. A T Nation thread on post-Accutane recovery links to a review of antiandrogenic progestogens.[31] Because the pill is only available to women by prescription and mostly outside English-speaking countries, it appears mainly in dermatology and gynaecology literature rather than in forum culture.
